problem:
Find where the normal line to the curve $y=3{x}^{2}-6x+5$ at the point $(0,5)$ intersects the $x$-axis.

The normal line intersects the $x$-axis at
$($
{{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}} $).$
worked_solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(3{x}^{2}-6x+5)=6x-6.
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{′}(0)=6(0)-6=-6,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(-6)}=\frac{1}{6}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-5 & =\frac{1}{6}(x-0) \\ y & =\frac{1}{6}x+5.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6}x+5 & =0 \\ \frac{1}{6}x & =-5 \\ x & =-30.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(\,-30,0\,).$
